canonical_statement: This annual clinical update reviews diagnosis, risk stratification, and management of multiple myeloma in 2026.
Multiple myeloma accounts for about 1% of all cancers and about 10% of hematologic malignancies; the review cites more than 36,000 new US cases and almost 11,000 deaths annually.
MGUS is present in approximately 5% of people older than 50 years and progresses to multiple myeloma or a related malignancy at about 1% per year.
The review reports SMM progression rates of about 10% per year for the first 5 years, 3% per year for the next 5 years, and 1.5% per year thereafter.
Multiple myeloma diagnosis requires at least 10% clonal bone marrow plasma cells or a biopsy-proven plasmacytoma plus at least one myeloma-defining event.

Myeloma-defining events include attributable CRAB features, clonal marrow plasma cells at least 60%, involved/uninvolved serum FLC ratio at least 100 with involved FLC at least 100 mg/L, or more than one focal MRI lesion.
In the abstract and diagnosis narrative, the FLC-ratio myeloma-defining event additionally requires urinary monoclonal protein excretion of at least 200 mg per 24 hours.

Table 1 defines CRAB thresholds as calcium more than 1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal or above 11 mg/dL; creatinine clearance below 40 mL/min or serum creatinine above 2 mg/dL; hemoglobin more than 2 g/dL below normal or below 10 g/dL; or at least one osteolytic lesion.
Plasma cell leukemia is defined in the review as multiple myeloma with at least 5% circulating plasma cells on a conventional peripheral blood smear.

The review recommends SPEP, serum immunofixation, and serum free light chain assay when multiple myeloma is suspected; mass spectrometry is presented as a more sensitive and specific alternative when available.

Bone disease is best assessed with low-dose whole-body CT or PET/CT, while MRI is emphasized for suspected SMM focal lesions, extramedullary disease, cord compression, or detailed evaluation of symptomatic areas.
Table 2 classifies approximately 45% of myeloma as hyperdiploid and approximately 40% as IgH-translocated disease.
The IMS/IMWG high-risk definition includes del(17p) and/or TP53 mutation, bi-allelic del(1p), high-risk IgH translocations paired with gain(1q) or del(1p), or gain(1q) plus del(1p).

The mSMART framework adds plasma cell leukemia, high S-phase, and extramedullary disease as high-risk markers and defines double-hit disease by meeting the cytogenetic high-risk definition through two factors.

The review reports median survival above 10 years in transplant-eligible patients with 4-year survival above 90%, and median survival around 7-8 years with 5-year survival above 70% among patients older than 65 years.
For most newly diagnosed transplant-eligible patients, the author favors an anti-CD38 plus VRd quadruplet, using Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd.

For standard-risk transplant-eligible patients, the author favors Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for 4 cycles followed by ASCT and maintenance, while allowing deferred ASCT in responding patients if stem cells are collected early.
For high-risk transplant-eligible patients, the author favors Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for 3-4 cycles followed by ASCT and maintenance.
Once-weekly subcutaneous bortezomib and dexamethasone 40 mg once weekly are preferred for most initial therapy unless rapid disease control is urgently needed.
All patients treated with lenalidomide require thrombosis prophylaxis; aspirin is described as adequate for most patients, with anticoagulation suggested for higher-risk patients.

For suspected light-chain cast nephropathy with acute renal failure, the author prefers daratumumab plus VCd together with plasma exchange or dialysis using a high-cutoff filter, continuing plasma exchange until serum FLC is below 50 mg/dL and then as needed.

In transplant-ineligible patients who are not frail, the author prefers Dara-VRd or Isa-VRd for approximately 6 months followed by maintenance; DRd or VRd are alternatives when quadruplets are not accessible.
In frail transplant-ineligible patients, the author prefers DRd or Isa-Rd for approximately 6 months followed by maintenance.
The review recommends considering ASCT in eligible patients; in standard-risk patients responding well, ASCT may be performed early or delayed until first relapse if stem cells are harvested early.
Tandem ASCT and post-ASCT consolidation are not recommended outside clinical trials.
Current maintenance for most patients is lenalidomide plus daratumumab or isatuximab.
The author recommends lenalidomide for 2 years in standard-risk myeloma and until progression or unacceptable toxicity in high-risk myeloma.
The author recommends anti-CD38 maintenance until progression, but states it can be stopped after 2 years in standard-risk post-ASCT patients who have been MRD-negative for at least 1 year.
Bortezomib plus lenalidomide is presented as an alternative maintenance option for high-risk myeloma.
Lenalidomide maintenance is associated in the review with a 2- to 3-fold increase in second cancers, warranting counseling and monitoring.
In IFM 2009 as summarized in Table 7, early ASCT increased median PFS from 36 to 50 months, while 8-year overall survival was 60% with delayed ASCT and 62% with early ASCT.
In DETERMINATION as summarized in Table 7, median PFS was 46 months with VRd versus 68 months with VRd-ASCT; 5-year overall survival was 79% versus 81% (p>0.99).
In PERSEUS as summarized in Table 7, 4-year PFS was 68% with VRd and 84% with Dara-VRd; 4-year overall survival was 90% in both arms.
In IMROZ as summarized in Table 7, 5-year PFS was 45% with VRd and 63% with Isa-VRd; 5-year overall survival was 66% versus 72%.
In CEPHEUS as summarized in Table 7, PFS at 54 months was 49.5% with VRd and 68.1% with Dara-VRd; 4-year overall survival was 72% versus 75%.
In MAIA as summarized in Table 7, 5-year PFS was 29% with Rd and 53% with DRd; 5-year overall survival was 53% versus 66% (overall-survival p=0.0013).

Relapse treatment selection is framed around timing of relapse, response to prior therapy, aggressiveness of relapse, and performance status, and triplet regimens should contain at least two drugs to which the patient is not refractory.

canonical_statement: Patients eligible for salvage ASCT should be considered if they have never had ASCT or if the first ASCT produced a remission of at least 36 months with maintenance.

canonical_statement: The author states that bispecific antibodies carry a high infection risk and recommends routine monthly IVIG regardless of immunoglobulin level.
Routine prophylactic tocilizumab is presented as a way to greatly reduce cytokine release syndrome when initiating bispecific antibodies.
The review suggests considering treatment discontinuation or delays after an excellent response to bispecific therapy, particularly after 6 months, to reduce toxicity.
Talquetamab targets GPRC5D and is positioned mainly for later lines or as bridging therapy because of dysgeusia, appetite loss, nail changes, skin rash, and weight loss.
CAR-T cell therapy with ide-cel or cilta-cel is a major option in relapsed myeloma and should be considered in first or second relapse as an alternative to BCMA-directed bispecific therapy.
At first relapse without anti-CD38 refractoriness, the author prefers cilta-cel or teclistamab-daratumumab; with anti-CD38 refractoriness, the author prefers cilta-cel or a BCMA-directed bispecific.
At second or later relapse, preferred options include CAR-T, bispecific antibodies, belantamab mafodotin, or standard triplets, selected according to prior therapy and refractoriness.
For disease refractory to IMiDs, proteasome inhibitors, anti-CD38 antibodies, and BCMA-directed approaches, the review lists talquetamab, venetoclax for t(11;14), or alkylator-based regimens.
If relapse occurs more than 24-36 months after stopping therapy, the author states that the previously successful initial regimen can be re-used when possible.
In KarMMa-3 as summarized in Table 9, ide-cel increased overall response from 42% to 71% and median PFS from 4.4 to 13.3 months versus standard regimens.
In CARTITUDE-4 as summarized in Table 9, overall response was 67% with standard regimens and 85% with cilta-cel; median PFS was 11.8 months with standard regimens and not reached with cilta-cel.
In DREAMM-7 as summarized in Table 9, median PFS was 13 months with DVd and 37 months with belantamab-Vd; overall response was 71% versus 83%.
In MajesTEC-3 as summarized in Table 9, 3-year PFS was 29.7% with DPd/DVd and 83.4% with teclistamab-daratumumab; 3-year overall survival was 65.0% versus 83.3%.
In MajesTEC-9 as summarized in Table 9, 18-month PFS was 26.9% with PVd/Kd and 69.8% with teclistamab; 18-month overall survival was 68.6% versus 79.2%.
In MonumenTAL-3 as summarized in Table 9, 2-year PFS was 51.2% with DPd, 77.6% with talquetamab-daratumumab, and 81.3% with talquetamab-daratumumab-pomalidomide.

Zoledronic acid or pamidronate are recommended for all patients, with an every-3-4-month schedule presented as potentially similarly protective with fewer side effects than monthly therapy; denosumab is an alternative, especially with significant renal dysfunction.

The review suggests levofloxacin prophylaxis for the first 2-3 months of initial therapy, Pneumocystis prophylaxis for long-term steroid or anti-CD38 therapy, and acyclovir or valacyclovir with proteasome inhibitors, anti-CD38 antibodies, or elotuzumab.
In Section 9, the review states SMM progression is approximately 10% per year for the first 5 years, 3% per year for the next 5 years, and 1% per year thereafter.
Mayo 2018 high-risk SMM is defined by any 2-3 of serum M protein above 2 g/dL, involved/uninvolved FLC ratio above 20, and bone marrow plasma cells above 20%.
The author recommends daratumumab for newly diagnosed high-risk SMM and observation without therapy for all other SMM, with daratumumab considered if disease evolves into high-risk SMM.
In AQUILA as summarized by the review, 5-year PFS was 63.1% with daratumumab versus 40.8% with active monitoring, corresponding to a reported 51% risk reduction (p<0.001).
